Regression Analysis Tables

Source: vignettes/articles/regression.qmd 
library(dplyr)
library(parameters)
library(performance)
library(apa7)
library(psych)
apa7_defaults(font_family = "Open Sans", line_spacing = 1.5)

The apa7 package is closely aligned with the easystats suite of packages for reporting statistical analyses. In most cases, it relies on easystats functions to do most of the hard work and then converts the output to APA style tables. For example, the easystats package parameters has a function model_parameters that takes regression fit objects and displays regression coefficient tables into a tibble that is displayed as a markdown table. The apa_parameters function converts the output of model_parameters into a tibble that is ready for apa_flextable to display as an APA-style table. The workflow has three steps:

  1. Make a regression model fit object with lm, glm, or a similar function.
  2. apa_parameters converts the fit object into a tibble using easystats functions.
  3. apa_flextable converts the tibble into an APA-style table.

Because step 2 returns a tibble, you can post-process it with dplyr before step 3. In Quarto and R Markdown documents, however, the output of apa_parameters is displayed as an APA-style table automatically, so step 3 is only needed when you want to customize the table or save it.

Linear Regression 

d <- sat.act |>
  mutate(
    gender = factor(
      gender,
      levels = 1:2,
      labels = c("Male", "Female")
    ),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = 0:5,
      labels =     c("None", "High School", "Some College", "Bachelor", "Master", "Doctorate")
    )
  ) |>
  tidyr::drop_na()

lm1 <- lm(ACT ~ age + gender, d)
lm2 <- update(lm1, . ~ . + education)
lm3 <- update(lm2, . ~ . + SATV + SATQ)

In the console, apa_parameters prints as an ordinary tibble, so you can inspect it. Here as_tibble is used to show that tibble in this document.

In a rendered document, the output of apa_parameters is displayed as a table without further processing.

apa_parameters(lm1)

The output is still a tibble, so ordinary dplyr verbs work. Pass the result to apa_flextable to customize the table. For example, to drop the intercept:

apa_parameters(lm1) |>
  filter(Variable != "Constant")

To compare nested models, pass a list. Model fit statistics (R2, change in R2, and the F test of the change) are added automatically.

apa_parameters(list(lm1, lm2, lm3))

Many hierarchical regression tables instead put R2 and its change in rows below each model’s coefficients. Use performance_layout = "rows":

apa_parameters(list(lm1, lm2, lm3), performance_layout = "rows")

Binary Logistic Regression

apa_parameters also accepts glm objects. The table reports coefficients on the link scale (B), their standard errors, the exponentiated coefficient, and the test statistic. For logistic regression, the exponentiated coefficient is the odds ratio (OR), and the test statistic is z.

The Cowles data set in the carData package (Cowles & Davis, 1987) has the neuroticism and extraversion scores of 1,421 introductory psychology students and whether they volunteered to take part in psychological research. Here, the odds of volunteering depend on extraversion, neuroticism, and sex:

d_volunteer <- carData::Cowles |>
  transmute(
    Volunteered = factor(volunteer, levels = c("no", "yes"), labels = c("No", "Yes")),
    Extraversion = extraversion,
    Neuroticism = neuroticism,
    Sex = factor(sex, levels = c("female", "male"), labels = c("Female", "Male"))
  )

glm1 <- glm(
  Volunteered ~ Extraversion + Neuroticism + Sex,
  data = d_volunteer,
  family = binomial
)
apa_parameters(glm1)

Exponentiated coefficients are added whenever the link function is logit or log. They are labeled OR for logit links, IRR (incidence rate ratio) for log links in count models, and RR (risk ratio) for log links in binomial models. Set exponentiate = FALSE to leave them out, or exponentiate = TRUE to add them for other links such as probit.

apa_parameters(glm1, exponentiate = FALSE)

To choose and order the columns, use predictor_parameters. Columns that the model does not report (for example, t for a model tested with z) are dropped silently.

apa_parameters(
  glm1,
  predictor_parameters = c("Parameter", "Exp_Coefficient", "z", "p")
)

As with lm, starred and bolded mark significant coefficients.

apa_parameters(glm1, starred = "Coefficient", bolded = "p")

Comparing logistic regression models

A list of glm models is displayed with a pseudo-R2 (Tjur’s for logistic regression, as chosen by performance::r2) and a likelihood ratio test of the change, because the binomial family has a fixed dispersion parameter.

glm0 <- glm(Volunteered ~ Extraversion, data = d_volunteer, family = binomial)
apa_parameters(list(glm0, glm1))

The model comparison can also be displayed separately with apa_performance_comparison.

apa_performance_comparison(list(glm0, glm1))

Multinomial Logistic Regression

When the outcome has more than two unordered categories, multinomial logistic regression (nnet::multinom) compares each category with a reference category, which is the first level of the outcome. The BEPS data set in the carData package (Fox & Andersen, 2006) has the votes of 1,525 people in the British Election Panel Study of 1997–2001 (Conservative, Labour, or Liberal Democrat), their attitudes toward European integration (from 1 to 11, with higher scores for more Eurosceptic attitudes), and their knowledge of the parties’ positions on European integration (from 0 to 3). Here, Conservative is the reference category:

d_vote <- carData::BEPS |>
  transmute(
    Vote = vote,
    Euroscepticism = Europe,
    Knowledge = political.knowledge
  )

multinom1 <- nnet::multinom(
  Vote ~ Euroscepticism + Knowledge,
  data = d_vote,
  trace = FALSE
)

apa_parameters(multinom1) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

Each comparison gets a heading row with its coefficients indented below it, and the exponentiated coefficients are odds ratios relative to the reference category. More Eurosceptic voters had lower odds of voting Labour or Liberal Democrat rather than Conservative, and so did voters who knew more about the parties’ positions on Europe. To compare the categories with another reference, reorder the levels of the outcome (e.g., with relevel) before fitting the model. With category_headings = FALSE, each row is labeled with its category instead (e.g., “Labour: Constant”).

Lists of multinomial models are compared with McFadden’s pseudo-R2 and likelihood ratio tests:

multinom0 <- nnet::multinom(Vote ~ Euroscepticism, data = d_vote, trace = FALSE)
apa_performance_comparison(list(multinom0, multinom1))

Count Regression

For Poisson and negative binomial regression, the exponentiated coefficients are incidence rate ratios (IRR). The quine data set in the MASS package (Venables & Ripley, 2002) has the number of days that 146 children in New South Wales, Australia, were absent from school in a year. Here, absences depend on the child’s sex and on whether the child was classified as an average or a slow learner:

d_absences <- MASS::quine |>
  transmute(
    Absences = Days,
    Sex = factor(Sex, levels = c("F", "M"), labels = c("Female", "Male")),
    Learner = factor(Lrn, levels = c("AL", "SL"), labels = c("Average", "Slow"))
  )

glm_pois <- glm(Absences ~ Sex + Learner, data = d_absences, family = poisson)
apa_parameters(glm_pois)

Quasi-families and other families with an estimated dispersion parameter are tested with t instead of z, and the degrees of freedom are shown in the column header. Nested models are compared with F tests instead of likelihood ratio tests. The absences vary much more than a Poisson model expects, so the quasi-Poisson standard errors are about four times as large, and neither predictor is significant.

glm_qpois <- glm(Absences ~ Sex + Learner, data = d_absences, family = quasipoisson)
apa_parameters(glm_qpois)

Zero-inflated and hurdle models

Counts often have more zeros than a Poisson or negative binomial model expects. A zero-inflated model (pscl::zeroinfl) adds a logistic model of excess zeros, which come from cases that could only be zero (e.g., people who would not have an affair under any circumstances). A hurdle model (pscl::hurdle) instead has a logistic model of whether the count is zero or positive, and a zero-truncated count model of the positive counts. Either way, apa_parameters puts each part under its own heading. Only the count model’s coefficients are exponentiated (IRR), because the zero model’s coefficients are log odds. The Affairs data set in the AER package, from a magazine survey analyzed by Fair (1978), has the number of extramarital affairs that 601 married people reported having in the past year. The counts were coded from response categories (0, 1, 2, and 3 times; 7 for 4 to 10 times; and 12 for monthly or more often), and 75% of them are zeros. Here, the number of affairs depends on how happy people rated their marriages (from 1, very unhappy, to 5, very happy) and how religious they were (from 1, anti-religious, to 5, very religious), and so does the probability of an excess zero:

data("Affairs", package = "AER")
d_affairs <- Affairs |>
  transmute(
    Affairs = affairs,
    Happiness = rating,
    Religiousness = religiousness
  )

zinb <- pscl::zeroinfl(
  Affairs ~ Happiness + Religiousness | Happiness + Religiousness,
  data = d_affairs,
  dist = "negbin"
)

apa_parameters(zinb) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

People who were happier in their marriages or more religious were more likely to be among those who would not have an affair at all, and happier people who did have affairs had fewer of them. The note names the count distribution, gives the negative binomial dispersion parameter (θ), and explains the zero model. For a hurdle model, the zero model’s heading is “Zero hurdle model”, and its coefficients are the log odds of a count greater than zero:

pscl::hurdle(
  Affairs ~ Happiness + Religiousness | Happiness + Religiousness,
  data = d_affairs,
  dist = "negbin"
) |>
  apa_parameters() |>
  apa_note()
[1] "The count model is zero-truncated negative binomial with dispersion parameter *θ* = 1.35, and its coefficients are on the log scale. Zero hurdle coefficients are log odds of a count greater than zero. *IRR* = incidence rate ratio."

apa_performance_comparison compares nested zero-inflated or hurdle models with likelihood ratio tests.

For nested counts, or counts with many zeros, negative binomial and zero-inflated mixed models fit with glmmTMB are described in the multilevel article.

Generalized Additive Models

Generalized additive models (GAMs), fit with mgcv::gam, let a predictor’s effect be a smooth curve instead of a straight line. The Wong data set in the carData package (Wong et al., 2001) has the performance IQ of 200 patients tested after they woke from a coma caused by a traumatic brain injury, with the number of days in the coma and the number of days between waking and testing. Some patients were tested more than once, so only each patient’s first test is kept. Here, performance IQ depends on smooth functions of the length of the coma and the time since waking:

d_coma <- carData::Wong |>
  arrange(id, days) |>
  distinct(id, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  transmute(
    IQ = piq,
    Coma = duration,
    Recovery = days
  )

fit_gam <- mgcv::gam(
  IQ ~ s(Coma) + s(Recovery),
  data = d_coma,
  method = "REML"
)

apa_parameters(fit_gam) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

The parametric terms (here, only the constant) have coefficients and t tests, as in other regression models. Each smooth term has its effective degrees of freedom (edf: 1 for a straight line, more for a curvier shape) and an approximate F test of whether the smooth differs from zero. Here, the smooth of the time since waking is nearly a straight line (edf close to 1), and the smooth of the coma’s length is curved: patients in longer comas had lower IQs, but the decline levels off after about two or three months of coma. For non-Gaussian families (e.g., family = binomial), the parametric terms are tested with z, the smooth terms with χ2, and exponentiated coefficients (e.g., OR) are added. Use terms = "parametric" or terms = "smooth" to show only one kind of term. Smooths of a factor-by variable (e.g., s(Coma, by = Sex)) get a row for each level.

apa_performance gives the adjusted R2 and the percentage of the deviance explained:

apa_performance(fit_gam)

The smooth terms are shrunk toward simpler shapes, so nested GAMs cannot be compared with the usual F or likelihood ratio tests. Lists of GAMs are compared by R2 and AIC instead.

Collinearity

apa_collinearity reports the variance inflation factor (VIF) and tolerance of each predictor, as computed by performance::check_collinearity. In the third ACT model above, the two SAT scores are correlated, but not enough to inflate their standard errors much:

apa_collinearity(lm3) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

Education has more than 1 degree of freedom, so its VIF is the generalized VIF, and the note says so. Add "SE_factor" to columns for VIF1/(2df), which can be compared across terms with different degrees of freedom. To bold large VIFs, set flag to your cutoff (e.g., flag = 5 or flag = 10). In models with interactions, the VIFs of the interaction and its components are high in part because product terms are correlated with their components, and the note explains that this does not affect the test of the interaction.

lm(ACT ~ SATV * SATQ, data = d) |>
  apa_collinearity(flag = 10) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

With centered predictors, these VIFs are small, and the note leaves this out.

lm(ACT ~ SATV * SATQ, data = datawizard::center(d)) |>
  apa_collinearity(flag = 10) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

Table Notes

A regression table often needs a note that defines its symbols and explains its stars. apa_parameters records how each table was made, and apa_note turns that record into note text. For the hierarchical regression above, the note defines the standardized coefficient and the change in R2 and explains the stars on the change in R2:

tbl_lm <- apa_parameters(list(lm1, lm2, lm3))
apa_note(tbl_lm)
[1] "&beta; = standardized coefficient; &Delta;*R*^2^ = change in *R*^2^. ^\\* ^*p* < .05. ^\\*\\* ^*p* < .01. ^\\*\\*\\* ^*p* < .001."

The note changes with the table. With robust standard errors (vcov) and confidence intervals, it says which standard errors were used and defines CI:

apa_parameters(
  lm3,
  predictor_parameters = c("Parameter", "Coefficient", "SE", "CI", "t", "df_error", "p"),
  vcov = "HC3"
) |>
  apa_note()
[1] "Standard errors are heteroskedasticity-consistent (HC3). CI = confidence interval."

For logistic regression, it defines the odds ratio. For count models, it defines the incidence rate ratio, and for ordinal models, it says that thresholds are not tested. For mixed models (lme4), it gives the method used to approximate the degrees of freedom of the t tests (Kenward–Roger by default).

apa_parameters(glm1, starred = "p") |>
  apa_note()
[1] "*OR* = odds ratio. ^\\* ^*p* < .05. ^\\*\\* ^*p* < .01. ^\\*\\*\\* ^*p* < .001."

The text is in markdown and does not start with “Note.” because apaquarto adds that. With apaquarto, use apa_note in the apa-note chunk option with !expr. Chunk options are evaluated before the chunk runs, so make the table in an earlier chunk (as tbl_lm was made above) and display it in the chunk with the note. Write it as apa7::apa_note, because in documents with cached chunks, chunk options can be evaluated before library(apa7) takes effect:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-lm-note
#| apa7-width: landscape
#| tbl-cap: Hierarchical Regression Predicting ACT Scores
#| apa-note: !expr apa7::apa_note(tbl_lm)
tbl_lm
```
Note. β = standardized coefficient; ΔR2 = change in R2. * p < .05. ** p < .01. *** p < .001.

Without apaquarto (e.g., in a plain Quarto or R Markdown document, or a table saved to Word with flextable::save_as_docx), apa_flextable can put the note below the table itself. With note = TRUE, it uses the note from apa_note; a character string is used as the note instead. The note is added after the column widths are set, so a long note does not stretch the table.

apa_parameters(glm1, starred = "p") |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

Do not use note with the apa-note chunk option, or the note will appear twice.

The definitions come from the abbreviation slot of each column’s format, so any column with a definition is defined in the note. Symbols such as SE and t have no definition by default. To add one, or to reword a definition, change the slot in the column_formats passed to apa_parameters (or set it for every table with apa7_defaults(column_formats = cf)):

cf <- column_formats()
cf$SE@abbreviation <- "standard error"
cf$Std_Coefficient@abbreviation <- "standardized regression coefficient"
apa_parameters(lm1, column_formats = cf) |>
  apa_note()
[1] "*SE* = standard error; &beta; = standardized regression coefficient."

The generated note is a starting point. Add to it with paste (e.g., paste(apa_note(tbl_lm), "Education was dummy coded with None as the reference group.")), or use collapse = NULL to get one sentence per element, so you can drop or reword sentences. apa_note reads an attribute of the table that dplyr functions such as mutate and filter keep but some operations (e.g., joins) drop, so call it on the table that apa_parameters returned.

Citations in notes

Some notes cite the articles that describe a method: for example, the notes of meta-analysis tables cite the articles on trim and fill and the multilevel I2, and the notes of lavaan model comparisons cite the article on the scaled χ2 difference test. In the console, and in documents without the references, the citations are written as text (e.g., “(Duval & Tweedie, 2000)”), which you would add to the reference list by hand.

To have the citations formatted and added to the reference list automatically, write the references that come with apa7 to the document’s folder in the setup chunk and list the file in the YAML header:

apa7::apa7_write_bib("apa7.bib")
bibliography: [references.bib, apa7.bib]

In a Quarto project, the bibliography can also be set for the whole project in _quarto.yml or for a folder in _metadata.yml, and apa7 finds it there.

When the document is rendered, apa_note writes each citation whose reference is in the document’s bibliography as a Pandoc citation key (e.g., [@duvalTrimFillSimple2000]), which Pandoc (or apaquarto) turns into a citation such as “(Duval & Tweedie, 2000)” and an entry in the reference list. This works for notes in the apa-note chunk option and from apa_flextable(note = TRUE). The keys are those that the Better BibTeX extension for Zotero makes, so references exported from Zotero work, too.

To choose the form yourself, use apa_note(tbl, citations = "keys") or citations = "text", or set it for all notes with options(apa7.citations = "keys"). Text is the right choice for tables saved directly to Word (e.g., with flextable::save_as_docx), because Pandoc never sees them.

Printing Options

The apa7.print option controls how the output of apa_parameters, apa_performance, and apa_performance_comparison is displayed.

  • "auto" (default): table in Quarto and R Markdown documents, tibble in the console.
  • "flextable": table everywhere.
  • "tibble": tibble everywhere.
options(apa7.print = "flextable")

To get the table with non-default settings, pass the output to apa_flextable, which always returns a flextable.
